case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: Inducement requires evidence of intent, not merely foreseeability of misuse. It does not disturb Sony where that evidence is absent.
case.holding: Distributing a tool with the object of promoting its use to infringe, shown by clear expression or affirmative steps, creates liability for the resulting infringement.

case.why_ai_cites_it: Cited by plaintiffs rather than defendants. It is the counterweight to Sony: capability of lawful use does not immunise a developer who markets or designs for infringement, which is why discovery in AI cases targets internal messages about training data.

reading.body:
MGM v. Grokster, a 2005 case holding that distributing a tool with the intent of promoting infringement creates liability, is cited by plaintiffs specifically, the counterweight to the defense-side precedents that dominate the rest of this collection.

It is quoted in four filings across two separate lawsuits, Cable News Network v. Perplexity AI and X.AI v. Ellison, by both plaintiffs and, in one filing, the defense itself, which shows this precedent is contested ground rather than settled in favor of either side. Its own stated limit narrows its actual reach. Inducement liability requires evidence of intent, not merely that a tool could foreseeably be misused, which is why the case record notes that discovery in AI lawsuits specifically targets internal company messages about training data as the evidence this standard requires.

The data does not report how any of the four filings resolved, only that this precedent's intent standard is what each side is arguing over.
